REASONS FOR DECISION

[1] XXXX XXXX (the principal claimant, hereinafter referred to as the P.C.), allegedly born in India of Tibetan parents, and her two minor sons, XXXX XXXX and XXXX XXXX XXXX, both citizens of the United States (US), are seeking refugee protection pursuant to ss. 96 and 97(1) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act (IRPA).

[2] The P.C. was appointed by the panel to act as designated representative on behalf of her minor sons. However, there was no evidence adduced with respect to their residency in the US. Accordingly, the panel finds that the minor children are not Convention refugees or persons in need of protection.
ALLEGATIONS

[3] The P.C.'s allegations are described in detail in her Personal Information Form (PIF).1 They can be summarized as follows.

[4] The P.C. was born in a Tibetan settlement in south India in 1972 and has lived there ever since. She was married in 1995 and has two children, who are included in this claim. In 1998, she was successful in obtaining a US visa and a year later her husband joined her in the US. Their two children were born in the US. Although the P.C. and her husband had a 2 year separation, the P.C. remained in the US undocumented. According to the P.C.'s PIF, following the birth of her first son, she applied for legal rights to remain in the US but was denied due to lack of evidence.

[5] The P.C. and her husband reunited and she gave birth to a second son. Given that the P.C. was undocumented, she is fearful that she will be deported to India and deported to Tibet as she alleges that she has no valid residence permit to remain in India. The P.C. fears persecution if sent to Tibet due to her religious beliefs as she is a follower of His Holiness the Dalai Lama.
DETERMINATION

[9] In considering credibility, the RPD is aware of the difficulties that may be faced by the claimant in establishing her claim, namely, the setting of the hearing room, and the stress inherent in responding to questions. Moreover, the RPD considered the passage of time of more than five years when examining the issue of credibility, and the ability to recall precise details of what has transpired over a lengthy period of time. The panel further considered the Chairperson's Guidelines with respect to female claimants fearing persecution, and in this regard, the RPD has applied these guidelines. The RPD's comments follow with respect to the P.C.'s lack of status in the U.S.
Status in the U.S.

[10] The claimant arrived in the US in 1998 on her own with a valid U.S. visitor's visa, which permitted her to remain in the US for 6 months. She told the authorities that she would be travelling on a tour with her siblings; however, with some prodding, she acknowledged that she had no intention of returning to India. Her husband followed a year later.

[11] She testified that she had no money when she arrived, so hence she delayed making a refugee claim. Due to the delay in filing her claim, the P.C. was ineligible; however, she made her husband aware of the one year requirement, and he was granted status. The P.C. submitted no documentation with respect to her husband. She believes that her husband was accepted as a Convention refugee in 2001. She further believes that it was approximately 2001 or 2002, when he wanted to sponsor her. However, she did not wish to return to India as her husband was having an affair, and in fact, they separated from 2003 until 2005. She then made a refugee claim in 2005. Accordingly, the RPD concludes that the P.C. had no status from 6 months after her arrival in the US until 2005 when she filed her refugee claim. The P.C's refugee claim was denied on October 2, 2007 and her appeal was dismissed on January 29, 2009, due to her failure to establish the timing of her entry into the country which would have established the timelines for filing her claim (one year after entry). In addition, it was denied due to adverse serious credibility findings4 which went to the heart of her claim. Counsel submits that her denial was due to lack of evidence, which the RPD categorically rejects. The panel acknowledges that the P.C. herself stated that "they did not believe me." The RPD further notes that the US authorities' statements with respect to inconsistencies surrounding the testimony went to the heart of her refugee claim.

[12] The panel asked the claimant why her husband did not pursue the sponsorship from 2009 until she left in 2012. She responded that her lawyer told her that given her lengthy undocumented US status she would not be successful. Hence, she arrived in Canada in 2012.

subthemes.text:
[16] The applicable jurisprudence as to whether Tibetans born in India between 1950 and 1987 have a right to citizenship in India is mixed. However, the panel has carefully considered the testimony, the documentation and submissions, and the Federal Court of Appeal decisions.
Right to Indian Citizenship

[17] Section 3(1) of the Indian Citizenship (Amendment) Act, 2003 states as follows:11
Except as provided in sub-section (2), every person born in India,
(a) On or after the 26th day of January, 1950, but before the 1st day of July, 1987;
(b) On or after the 1st day of July, 1987 but before the commencement of the Citizenship (Amendment) Act, 2003, and either of whose parents is a citizen of India at the time of his birth;
(c) on or after the commencement of the Citizenship (Amendment) Act, 2003, where
(i) both of his parents are citizens of India; or
(ii) one of whose parents is a citizen of India and the other is not an illegal migrant at the time of his birth,
shall be a citizen of India by birth.

[18] Pursuant to this statute, the P.C. was born in India in 1972 which is between the applicable dates as stated above. However, it is argued that the documentation submitted by the P.C. supports the assertion that in reality Indian citizenship is not automatically granted and there are in fact hindrances to obtaining said citizenship.12

[19] The panel has examined the recent decisions of the High Court of Delhi and the Karnataka High Court. The decision of the Delhi High Court referred to the case of Namgyal Dolkar, a Tibetan woman born in India on 13 April, 1986. Ms. Dolkar petitioned to overturn the decision of the Ministry of External Affairs to deny her an Indian passport. The Court found that Ms. Dolkar was entitled to claim Indian citizenship by birth pursuant to the Citizenship Act and, as such, could not be denied a passport. The Court subsequently ordered the Ministry of External Affairs to process Ms. Dolkar's passport application and further issued a fine against the Ministry. The Court further ruled that a person who is an Indian citizen by birth is not required to apply for citizenship.13

[20] Notwithstanding the foregoing, the P.C. argues that, as a Tibetan resident in India, who does not have proper identity documents, e.g. registration certificate and identity certificate issued by the Indian Government, she would be unable to obtain citizenship in any circumstances.

[21] The RPD is not persuaded by the P.C.'s arguments and the affidavits submitted in support of this argument. It is clear from the decisions of the High Court that, as an ethnic Tibetan born in India between January 26, 1950 and July 1, 1987, the P.C. is an Indian citizen by birth, irrespective of the nationality of his/her parents, and that there is no need to apply for citizenship as citizenship is automatically acquired by birth. The RPD notes that there are cases that reveal difficulties for some ethnic Tibetans in acquiring passports; however, these cases do not serve to establish that citizenship is not in their control.
Has the P.C. attempted to obtain Indian citizenship?

[22] The claimant testified that at no time did she attempt to obtain Indian citizenship while in India. The panel notes that the claimant was 27 years of age when she left India, and yet she made no attempts prior to her departure to obtain any documents to acquire citizenship. She further submits that she has lost or misplaced her identity documents, which she believes she discovered in 2007 while in the U.S. She was asked if she had made any efforts to replace them or any inquiries with respect to her options. She responded that she had not thought of replacing the lost documents, and she believed that she had to be present in India to apply for these documents.

[23] The RPD notes that the National Documentation package for China states:
Tibetans who are born in India receive their initial RCs at the age of sixteen. In general, a birth certificate is required to obtain an RC; however, a child who does not have a birth certificate may also show school documents (their Class 10 certificate) or prove his or her identity through police certification.14

[24] The only effort that the claimant made was two months ago, according to her testimony. She stated that she went to the Indian Embassy here in Toronto to inquire as to how she could obtain a passport. She was told to go "on line" and then she learned that she required accompanying identification documents, which she no longer has in her possession. The RPD notes that the P.C. left India in 1989 and yet her one and only attempt to obtain documents was two months prior to her hearing. When confronted with this by the panel, the P.C. was unable to proffer an explanation. Furthermore, she stated that she had no proof that she had attended the Embassy as she did not have an appointment, and she further asserted that the Embassy will not provide any such proof. By contrast, the panel notes that when the P.C.'s husband suggested she return to India for him to initiate a sponsorship, at no time did she indicate that lack of documentation would preclude this.

The RPD prefers the documentary evidence indicating that educational documents, PAN Card, Aadhar Card, election identity card and driver's licence can be used in lieu of a birth certificates, over the claimant's testimony that she is required to have her misplaced or lost identity certificates. The claimant in response to counsel stated that she does not have either a PAN Card or an Aadhar Card. However, the RPD notes that she has 13 years of education and no evidence was proffered in this regard. The RPD finds that the P.C.'s testimony as to the requirements to obtain a passport is not in line with the documentary evidence. In conclusion, the RPD finds that the documentary evidence is more reliable, being sourced from governmental institutions in Canada, U.S. and India that are expected to be knowledgeable about this issue. More importantly, is the fact, that by the P.C's own acknowledgment, she made no contacts whatsoever as to how she could obtain documents and therefore, she has been unable to provide to the panel any impediments in procuring her citizenship.
Federal Court

[26] The majority decision of the Federal Court of Appeal in Tretsetsang16 outlined that is open to the Board to draw reasonable inferences from the failure of a claimant to take reasonable steps to acquire citizenship. It stated that where an impediment is alleged to exist, a claimant must show on a balance of probabilities the following:
* The existence of a significant impediment that may reasonably be considered capable of preventing the claimant from exercising his or her citizenship rights of state protection in that country of nationality; and
* That the claimant has made reasonable efforts to overcome such impediment and that such efforts were unsuccessful such that the claimant was unable to obtain the protection of that state.

subthemes.text:
[27] The court in Tretsetsang further determined that:
If a claimant alleges that he or she is unable to access state protection from the country of which he or she is a citizen and fails to take any steps to confirm whether that country will recognize the claimant as a citizen of that country, such inaction, in the absence of a reasonable explanation, would be fatal to that person's refugee claim.17

[28] This was re-iterated in the Dakar case, where the Federal Court found that the applicant had not made reasonable efforts to acquire his Indian citizenship.18

[29] The analysis in Tretsetsang is consistent with and expands upon the reasoning in Williams in terms of making reasonable attempts to avail oneself of citizenship and obstacles and inconvenience, in themselves, are insufficient to overcome this obligation.

[30] As stated above, the claimant made no attempt while in India to acquire citizenship, and after her arrival in the US and Canada, she allegedly lost her residency and identity certificates, but made no contact with anyone with respect to documents until two months prior to the hearing, after being out of India for 19 years.

[31] Although not determinative, the panel cannot help but consider the credibility findings with respect to the P.C's undocumented stay in the U.S. The panel rejects the explanations provided by the P.C. Moreover, the Panel finds, contrary to counsel's submission, that the delay of more than one year in filing her refugee claim is merely an excuse for some serious credibility concerns surrounding her refugee claim.

[32] At the very least, the P.C.'s actions and lack of credibility with the Immigration authorities in the US, cannot help but detract from her overall credibility, which includes the loss of her documents and even her efforts with the Embassy, which in any event, were a last ditch effort.

[33] The RPD concludes that India is a country of reference in this claim and the P.C. fears deportation to China. She does not alleges that she faces a serious possibility of persecution pursuant to section 96 nor that she is a person in need of protection pursuant to section 97(1) of the IRPA.
CONCLUSION

[34] Accordingly, the RPD finds that the P.C. is not a Convention refugee or a person in need of protection, and as stated above, nor are her minor children, as they were born in the US. These claims are rejected.

REASONS FOR DECISION

[1] XXXX XXXX (the principal claimant, hereinafter referred to as the P.C.), allegedly born in India of Tibetan parents, and her two minor sons, XXXX XXXX and XXXX XXXX XXXX, both citizens of the United States (US), are seeking refugee protection pursuant to ss. 96 and 97(1) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act (IRPA).

[2] The P.C. was appointed by the panel to act as designated representative on behalf of her minor sons. However, there was no evidence adduced with respect to their residency in the US. Accordingly, the panel finds that the minor children are not Convention refugees or persons in need of protection.
ALLEGATIONS
[3] The P.C.'s allegations are described in detail in her Personal Information Form (PIF).1 They can be summarized as follows.

[4] The P.C. was born in a Tibetan settlement in south India in 1972 and has lived there ever since. She was married in 1995 and has two children, who are included in this claim. In 1998, she was successful in obtaining a US visa and a year later her husband joined her in the US. Their two children were born in the US. Although the P.C. and her husband had a 2 year separation, the P.C. remained in the US undocumented. According to the P.C.'s PIF, following the birth of her first son, she applied for legal rights to remain in the US but was denied due to lack of evidence.

[5] The P.C. and her husband reunited and she gave birth to a second son. Given that the P.C. was undocumented, she is fearful that she will be deported to India and deported to Tibet as she alleges that she has no valid residence permit to remain in India. The P.C. fears persecution if sent to Tibet due to her religious beliefs as she is a follower of His Holiness the Dalai Lama.
DETERMINATION

[6] The RPD finds that the P.C. has not satisfied the burden of establishing a serious possibility of persecution on a Convention ground, or that, on a balance of probabilities, she would personally be subjected to a risk to life, or a risk of cruel and unusual treatment or punishment or a danger of torture.
DETERMINATIVE ISSUES

[7] The determinative issues are credibility, residency in the US, country of reference, and the P.C.'s efforts and ability to acquire Indian citizenship.
Identity

[8] The RPD had some concerns about the P.C.'s identity. However, the panel finds that based on a copy of her Green Book2 and letters from the Dhondenling Tibetan Settlement office (CTA),3 which indicate that she was born in India on XXXX XXXX, 1972, the RPD finds, on a balance of probabilities, that she is a Tibetan who has resided in India since birth.
Credibility

[9] In considering credibility, the RPD is aware of the difficulties that may be faced by the claimant in establishing her claim, namely, the setting of the hearing room, and the stress inherent in responding to questions. Moreover, the RPD considered the passage of time of more than five years when examining the issue of credibility, and the ability to recall precise details of what has transpired over a lengthy period of time. The panel further considered the Chairperson's Guidelines with respect to female claimants fearing persecution, and in this regard, the RPD has applied these guidelines. The RPD's comments follow with respect to the P.C.'s lack of status in the U.S.
Status in the U.S.

[10] The claimant arrived in the US in 1998 on her own with a valid U.S. visitor's visa, which permitted her to remain in the US for 6 months. She told the authorities that she would be travelling on a tour with her siblings; however, with some prodding, she acknowledged that she had no intention of returning to India. Her husband followed a year later.

[11] She testified that she had no money when she arrived, so hence she delayed making a refugee claim. Due to the delay in filing her claim, the P.C. was ineligible; however, she made her husband aware of the one year requirement, and he was granted status. The P.C. submitted no documentation with respect to her husband. She believes that her husband was accepted as a Convention refugee in 2001. She further believes that it was approximately 2001 or 2002, when he wanted to sponsor her. However, she did not wish to return to India as her husband was having an affair, and in fact, they separated from 2003 until 2005. She then made a refugee claim in 2005. Accordingly, the RPD concludes that the P.C. had no status from 6 months after her arrival in the US until 2005 when she filed her refugee claim. The P.C's refugee claim was denied on October 2, 2007 and her appeal was dismissed on January 29, 2009, due to her failure to establish the timing of her entry into the country which would have established the timelines for filing her claim (one year after entry). In addition, it was denied due to adverse serious credibility findings4 which went to the heart of her claim. Counsel submits that her denial was due to lack of evidence, which the RPD categorically rejects. The panel acknowledges that the P.C. herself stated that "they did not believe me." The RPD further notes that the US authorities' statements with respect to inconsistencies surrounding the testimony went to the heart of her refugee claim.

[12] The panel asked the claimant why her husband did not pursue the sponsorship from 2009 until she left in 2012. She responded that her lawyer told her that given her lengthy undocumented US status she would not be successful. Hence, she arrived in Canada in 2012.

[13] The panel concludes that the P.C. was without status in the US for 7/8 years. Moreover, it was only after much prodding, that this evidence was elicited. Furthermore, the RPD finds that the information contained in the US court's appeal judgment5 calls the P.C.'s credibility into question. The lack of corroborative evidence is also noteworthy, i.e. no information about the P.C.'s husband's claim and no evidence to support the alleged legal consultation.

[14] This aspect of the claimant's conduct is also inconsistent with a person living in fear of persecution in their country. It is to be expected that genuine Convention refugees would seek protection as soon as is practical, once out of reach of their oppressors. The Board is mindful, then, that one of the significant factors which speaks to subjective fear and credibility is the element of delay. Delay, in and of itself, is not normally a decisive factor in refugee determination.6 However, it can be relevant and a potentially important consideration to the Board,7 where the claimant has delayed in making a claim and failed to offer a reasonable explanation for the delay. In certain circumstances, however, delay can be a determinative and decisive factor.8 In the case at hand, the Board draws an adverse inference and finds as a result of that delay, the P.C.'s credibility is seriously undermined.
Countries of Reference

[15] When a claimant has citizenship that is available to her in another safe country and it is within her power to acquire said citizenship, a claim for refugee protection may be denied.9 In applying the principles espoused in Williams,10 the RPD must consider the degree of control that the claimant has over the process of obtaining citizenship.

[16] The applicable jurisprudence as to whether Tibetans born in India between 1950 and 1987 have a right to citizenship in India is mixed. However, the panel has carefully considered the testimony, the documentation and submissions, and the Federal Court of Appeal decisions.
Right to Indian Citizenship

[17] Section 3(1) of the Indian Citizenship (Amendment) Act, 2003 states as follows:11
Except as provided in sub-section (2), every person born in India,
(a) On or after the 26th day of January, 1950, but before the 1st day of July, 1987;
(b) On or after the 1st day of July, 1987 but before the commencement of the Citizenship (Amendment) Act, 2003, and either of whose parents is a citizen of India at the time of his birth;
(c) on or after the commencement of the Citizenship (Amendment) Act, 2003, where
(i) both of his parents are citizens of India; or
(ii) one of whose parents is a citizen of India and the other is not an illegal migrant at the time of his birth,
shall be a citizen of India by birth.

[18] Pursuant to this statute, the P.C. was born in India in 1972 which is between the applicable dates as stated above. However, it is argued that the documentation submitted by the P.C. supports the assertion that in reality Indian citizenship is not automatically granted and there are in fact hindrances to obtaining said citizenship.12

[19] The panel has examined the recent decisions of the High Court of Delhi and the Karnataka High Court. The decision of the Delhi High Court referred to the case of Namgyal Dolkar, a Tibetan woman born in India on 13 April, 1986. Ms. Dolkar petitioned to overturn the decision of the Ministry of External Affairs to deny her an Indian passport. The Court found that Ms. Dolkar was entitled to claim Indian citizenship by birth pursuant to the Citizenship Act and, as such, could not be denied a passport. The Court subsequently ordered the Ministry of External Affairs to process Ms. Dolkar's passport application and further issued a fine against the Ministry. The Court further ruled that a person who is an Indian citizen by birth is not required to apply for citizenship.13

[20] Notwithstanding the foregoing, the P.C. argues that, as a Tibetan resident in India, who does not have proper identity documents, e.g. registration certificate and identity certificate issued by the Indian Government, she would be unable to obtain citizenship in any circumstances.

[21] The RPD is not persuaded by the P.C.'s arguments and the affidavits submitted in support of this argument. It is clear from the decisions of the High Court that, as an ethnic Tibetan born in India between January 26, 1950 and July 1, 1987, the P.C. is an Indian citizen by birth, irrespective of the nationality of his/her parents, and that there is no need to apply for citizenship as citizenship is automatically acquired by birth. The RPD notes that there are cases that reveal difficulties for some ethnic Tibetans in acquiring passports; however, these cases do not serve to establish that citizenship is not in their control.
Has the P.C. attempted to obtain Indian citizenship?

[22] The claimant testified that at no time did she attempt to obtain Indian citizenship while in India. The panel notes that the claimant was 27 years of age when she left India, and yet she made no attempts prior to her departure to obtain any documents to acquire citizenship. She further submits that she has lost or misplaced her identity documents, which she believes she discovered in 2007 while in the U.S. She was asked if she had made any efforts to replace them or any inquiries with respect to her options. She responded that she had not thought of replacing the lost documents, and she believed that she had to be present in India to apply for these documents.

[23] The RPD notes that the National Documentation package for China states:
Tibetans who are born in India receive their initial RCs at the age of sixteen. In general, a birth certificate is required to obtain an RC; however, a child who does not have a birth certificate may also show school documents (their Class 10 certificate) or prove his or her identity through police certification.14

The RPD notes that the P.C. left India in 1989 and yet her one and only attempt to obtain documents was two months prior to her hearing. When confronted with this by the panel, the P.C. was unable to proffer an explanation. Furthermore, she stated that she had no proof that she had attended the Embassy as she did not have an appointment, and she further asserted that the Embassy will not provide any such proof. Federal Court

[26] The majority decision of the Federal Court of Appeal in Tretsetsang16 outlined that is open to the Board to draw reasonable inferences from the failure of a claimant to take reasonable steps to acquire citizenship. It stated that where an impediment is alleged to exist, a claimant must show on a balance of probabilities the following:
* The existence of a significant impediment that may reasonably be considered capable of preventing the claimant from exercising his or her citizenship rights of state protection in that country of nationality; and
* That the claimant has made reasonable efforts to overcome such impediment and that such efforts were unsuccessful such that the claimant was unable to obtain the protection of that state.

[27] The court in Tretsetsang further determined that:
If a claimant alleges that he or she is unable to access state protection from the country of which he or she is a citizen and fails to take any steps to confirm whether that country will recognize the claimant as a citizen of that country, such inaction, in the absence of a reasonable explanation, would be fatal to that person's refugee claim.17
[28] This was re-iterated in the Dakar case, where the Federal Court found that the applicant had not made reasonable efforts to acquire his Indian citizenship.18

[29] The analysis in Tretsetsang is consistent with and expands upon the reasoning in Williams in terms of making reasonable attempts to avail oneself of citizenship and obstacles and inconvenience, in themselves, are insufficient to overcome this obligation.

[30] As stated above, the claimant made no attempt while in India to acquire citizenship, and after her arrival in the US and Canada, she allegedly lost her residency and identity certificates, but made no contact with anyone with respect to documents until two months prior to the hearing, after being out of India for 19 years.

[31] Although not determinative, the panel cannot help but consider the credibility findings with respect to the P.C's undocumented stay in the U.S. The panel rejects the explanations provided by the P.C. Moreover, the Panel finds, contrary to counsel's submission, that the delay of more than one year in filing her refugee claim is merely an excuse for some serious credibility concerns surrounding her refugee claim.

[32] At the very least, the P.C.'s actions and lack of credibility with the Immigration authorities in the US, cannot help but detract from her overall credibility, which includes the loss of her documents and even her efforts with the Embassy, which in any event, were a last ditch effort.

[33] The RPD concludes that India is a country of reference in this claim and the P.C. fears deportation to China. She does not alleges that she faces a serious possibility of persecution pursuant to section 96 nor that she is a person in need of protection pursuant to section 97(1) of the IRPA.
CONCLUSION

[34] Accordingly, the RPD finds that the P.C. is not a Convention refugee or a person in need of protection, and as stated above, nor are her minor children, as they were born in the US. These claims are rejected.
